lesson_title: The GIS in Your Pocket: Layers, Satellites and the Census
hook_text: Search 'pizza near me' and you just ran the same technology that plans clinics and counts the country.
clip_script: Open the map on your phone and search for pizza. Blue dot, red pins, a route drawing itself. Congratulations — you just ran a full Geographical Information System. Captures, stores, analyses, displays information tied to positions on the earth. Same definition, word for word. Now the trick that makes it powerful: layers. Imagine South Africa's rivers drawn on one transparent sheet. Roads on a second. Clinics on a third. Population density shaded on a fourth. Stack them and hold the pile to the light — and suddenly a crowded community with NO clinic nearby jumps straight off the page. That is overlay analysis, and it is how planners decide where the next clinic, standpipe or school actually goes. Where does the data come from? A lot of it from space. Satellites pass over the same spot every few days, so new tin roofs on a city's edge appear between images — growth you can measure from orbit. But here is the limit: a satellite counts ROOFS, never people. It cannot ask who lives below, or their age, or their language. For that, a human being still knocks on the door. The eye in the sky sees everywhere. The census asks everything. Together, they map the nation.
visual_style: Phone screen zooming out into stacked transparent map layers over South Africa; time-lapse satellite frames showing roofs multiplying; a final split of satellite view and a door being knocked.
pacing: Fast familiar hook, slow satisfying layer-stack, punchy roof-counting twist to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to master GIS components and remote sensing for the exam.
